title: Shakespeare’s Sonnets
author: William Shakespeare
written: Between about 1591 and 1604, over more than a decade
setting: No place is named for most of the sequence. What the poems have instead is a situation: a poet, a young man he cannot claim in public, a woman they share, and a period of absence long enough to write in
lengthNote: 154 poems, 2,155 lines. All but three keep to fourteen lines: 99 has fifteen, 126 has twelve, and 145 is in shorter lines throughout
openingLine: From fairest creatures we desire increase,
summary: A poet spends seventeen poems telling a beautiful young man to have a child, then changes his argument: the poems themselves will keep him. What follows is a long record of that claim being tested — by absence, by a rival poet, by the young man's own behaviour, and by a woman the poet desires and does not admire. The sequence ends with poems about lust, lying and self-disgust that are as plain as the early ones are ornate. Read in the 1609 order, it is the most sustained piece of writing Shakespeare left outside the plays, and the only one written in the first person.
referenceStyle: sonnet number and line, following the 1609 quarto's numbering

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of Shakespeare’s Sonnets (eBook 1041)
sourceText.note: A modern-spelling text in the 1609 order. It keeps elided forms such as ruin’d and show’st, and at 126.2 it prints “his fickle hour” where many editions read “his sickle, hour”. Quotations here follow it exactly.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Two of the poems were in print by 1599 and Francis Meres had heard of the others by 1598, so the sequence was long in the making.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Thomas Thorpe entered SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS in the Stationers' Register on 20 May 1609. Whether Shakespeare authorised it is still argued.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg — the form Surrey devised and Shakespeare made his own.

atAGlance.label: Address
atAGlance.note: Sonnets 1-126 are addressed to or about a young man; 127-152 concern a woman. The last two are translations of a Greek epigram.

structure.label: Sonnets 1-17
structure.title: The procreation sonnets
structure.summary: Seventeen poems make one request in seventeen ways: the young man should marry and father a son, because beauty that is not copied is beauty thrown away. The reasoning is economic as often as it is romantic — usury, husbandry, accounts, the unused estate. The group matters less for what it urges than for what it establishes: a speaker whose subject is time, and a listener who never answers.

scenes.title: Increase
scenes.summary: The first line states the whole sequence's problem — we want beautiful things to continue — and the first accusation follows: the young man is at war with himself, feeding his own light and starving the world.

scenes.title: The glass
scenes.summary: Look in the mirror and see your mother's April. The argument makes family resemblance evidence that a face is not private property.

scenes.title: The clock
scenes.summary: The first great time poem: clock, violet, sable curls, harvest. Nothing defends against time except breeding, and the couplet says so with the coldness of a proverb.

scenes.title: The graft
scenes.summary: The turn that makes the rest possible. War with Time is declared, and the weapon is no longer a child but the poem itself.

scenes.title: Twice
scenes.summary: The doubt inside the boast: future readers will call the poems liars sooner than believe in such a face. A child would prove it — 'you should live twice'.

structure.label: Sonnets 18-60
structure.title: The poems in place of a child
structure.summary: Once verse takes the child's place, the writing changes: the praise gets stranger, the confidence louder, and the first damage appears. Sonnet 20 makes the addressee's beauty a problem of gender; 33-35 forgive a betrayal the poems never describe; 55 raises the monument. The group ends on the sequence's plainest statement of loss, waves moving up a beach.

scenes.title: The summer's day
scenes.summary: The most famous poem in English begins as a comparison and ends as a contract: the lines breathe, therefore he does.

scenes.title: The master mistress
scenes.summary: A woman's face, a man's body, nature changing her mind mid-poem. The couplet's joke about what nature added is also a division of the property: love to the speaker, use to women.

scenes.title: Disgrace
scenes.summary: Envy, self-hatred, then a single remembered person, and the lark. The volta is the clearest demonstration in the sequence of what a turn can do.

scenes.title: The morning
scenes.summary: The sun flatters the mountains and then hides. The poem forgives the young man by making him weather, which is generous and not quite honest.

scenes.title: The monument
scenes.summary: Marble and gilded monuments against 'this powerful rhyme'. The boast is conventional; the survival of the poem is not.

scenes.title: The waves
scenes.summary: Minutes as waves on a shingle beach, each taking the place of the one before. The couplet's only defence is the verse, stated without triumph.

structure.label: Sonnets 61-103
structure.title: Absence, a rival, and a fault confessed
structure.summary: The middle of the sequence is where it stops being praise. A rival poet appears with better patronage and a louder style; the young man's affection is withdrawn; the speaker is older than his subject and says so. The poems become defensive, ironic, and in places wounded. The best of them — 73, 87, 94 — are about being left.

scenes.title: That time of year
scenes.summary: Autumn, twilight, embers: three images of ending, each shorter than the last, so the poem itself runs out of time as it describes running out of time.

scenes.title: The rival
scenes.summary: A better spirit uses the young man's name. The speaker casts himself as a small boat beside a ship, which is modest and competitive.

scenes.title: Farewell
scenes.summary: A whole poem in the language of property law — dear, estimate, charter, patent, bonds. Love ends as a contract found void.

scenes.title: Lilies
scenes.summary: The most withholding poem in the sequence. Cold, unmoved people are praised for three quatrains, and the couplet drops a smell into the room.

structure.label: Sonnets 104-126
structure.title: Constancy argued, and the envoy
structure.summary: The last movement addressed to the young man argues for a love that does not alter, and knows the argument is hard to believe. Sonnet 116 states it as law; 121 answers the people who judge him; 126 stops. Twelve lines, six couplets, no fourteenth line — the sequence's only unfinished poem, and it is unfinished on purpose.

scenes.title: The chronicle
scenes.summary: Old poems praising dead beauties were prophecies of this face. Praise becomes literary history, and the present tense is the one thing the old writers lacked.

scenes.title: The marriage of true minds
scenes.summary: Definition by negation: what love is not. Read at weddings; written, on the evidence of its neighbours, by a man being left.

scenes.title: The audit
scenes.summary: Nature can delay Time but not cancel the account. The poem ends two lines early, with empty brackets in the quarto where the couplet should be.

structure.label: Sonnets 127-154
structure.title: The dark lady sonnets
structure.summary: The last group changes subject, tone and manners. The woman is desired and not admired; the praise is a running argument with the conventions of praise; and the poems about lust are the most self-disgusted in English. Two of them treat the triangle directly — she has the young man too. The final pair, about Cupid's brand and a bath, translate a Greek epigram and read like a shrug.

scenes.title: Black
scenes.summary: The opening move of the group: beauty is now black, and the beauty industry of painted faces is the thing being mocked.

scenes.title: The expense of spirit
scenes.summary: Fourteen lines with barely a verb of action and no pronoun until the couplet. Lust before, during and after, described as a trap everyone can see and nobody avoids.

scenes.title: My mistress' eyes
scenes.summary: A catalogue of everything she is not, which turns out to demolish Petrarchan comparison, not her.

scenes.title: Lies
scenes.summary: Two people agreeing to believe each other's lies about age and fidelity. An earlier version had appeared in print in 1599.

scenes.title: Two loves
scenes.summary: The triangle stated as a morality play: the better angel, the worse, and a speaker who will only know the outcome when one fires the other out.

scenes.title: Perjury
scenes.summary: The sequence's last word to her is an admission that his own oaths were the worse ones. Eyes that swore against what they saw.

characters.name: The speaker
characters.role: The poet of the sequence, writing in the first person
characters.summary: An older man, publicly of lower rank than the person he writes to, who makes his living by writing and is ashamed of how. He is at his best when he is losing: the poems of praise are brilliant, the poems of abandonment are better. He lies to himself in the last group and says so in the same line.
characters.clue: Calls his own name a brand upon his hand, and puns on it until the word means desire, a man and a signature together.

relationships.label: outwritten by, or fears he is

characters.name: The young man
characters.role: The addressee of sonnets 1-126, never named
characters.summary: Beautiful, well born, and silent for 126 poems. He is urged to breed, then promised immortality instead; he takes another poet’s attention, takes the speaker’s mistress, and is forgiven in language that cannot stop noticing it is forgiving. Nothing in the sequence is told from his side, which is why readers keep inventing one.
characters.clue: Addressed as the master mistress of the speaker's passion, and as a lovely boy holding Time's glass.

relationships.label: shares a bed with, in the speaker's account

characters.name: The woman
characters.summary: Black-haired, black-eyed, married, musical, and unfaithful — that is the whole of what the poems establish. She is desired without being idealised, which makes the praise of her more convincing than the praise of the young man and the insults harder to forgive. The name readers use for her comes from later critics, not from the poems.
characters.clue: Her eyes are nothing like the sun, and the speaker swears she is fair while knowing she is not.

relationships.label: desired by, lies to and with

characters.name: The rival poet
characters.role: A competitor for the young man's attention in sonnets 78-86
characters.summary: A better-funded, grander-sounding writer whose verse the speaker describes as a full-sailed ship beside his own small boat. Whether he is Chapman, Marlowe or nobody at all, his function is exact: he makes praise a market, and makes the speaker admit that his poems have a price as well as a subject.
characters.clue: His 'great verse' is bound for the young man, and the speaker's tongue is tied when he hears it.

characters.name: Time
characters.summary: Given a scythe, a sickle, a pen, a hand and an appetite, Time is the one figure that appears in every group. It is addressed directly, insulted, bargained with and finally not defeated: the poems claim to outlast it, and the claim is the only weapon they have.
characters.clue: Called devouring, bloody, and a tyrant; asked to blunt its own lion's paws.

themes.name: Time
themes.summary: Time is not a mood in these poems, it is an opponent with a body: it has a scythe, a hand, a pen, and it eats. Almost every poem measures something against it — a face, a season, a clock, waves reaching a beach — and the only defence ever offered is a sheet of paper.
themes.development: The early poems propose a child as the answer; sonnet 15 replaces the child with the verse; by 60 and 65 the verse is a slim hope, no longer a victory; and 126 hands the young man to Time’s accountant without an argument.

themes.name: Poetry and immortality
themes.summary: The sequence is unusually frank about writing as work: contracts, accounts, monuments, invoices, borrowed styles, the rival's better-funded verse. The claim that the poems will preserve their subject is repeated so often that it stops being a boast and becomes a question.
themes.development: Confidence rises to the monument of 55, is undercut by the rival poems at 78-86, and is dropped without comment in the last group, where nobody promises anybody immortality.

themes.name: Love
themes.summary: Love here is rarely mutual and never safe. It is argued for, defended in the language of the law courts, withdrawn without explanation, and defined by what it will not do.
themes.development: The young man is addressed as a possession in the early poems, as an equal in the middle, and in 87 as an estate that was never really the speaker's; 116 then defines love as the thing that does not move, which the surrounding poems keep disproving.

themes.name: Desire and shame
themes.summary: The last group separates wanting from admiring and looks at what is left. Sonnet 129 describes lust in the three tenses of its own trap — before, during, after — and finds the same person in each.
themes.development: Desire is decorative in the first hundred poems and physical in the last twenty-five; the shame arrives with the physical detail and does not leave.

themes.name: Gender and beauty
themes.summary: Sonnet 20 gives the young man a woman's face and a man's body and makes a joke of nature changing her mind. The praise poems use the vocabulary reserved for women, and the sequence's one extended piece of female portraiture is a refusal of that vocabulary.
themes.development: The 1640 edition changed pronouns to make some of these poems address a woman, which is the clearest evidence of how uncomfortable they were; modern editions restore them.

themes.name: Rank
themes.summary: The speaker writes upwards. Patronage, service, disgrace with fortune, a public trade that has stained his name: the difference in station comes up often enough to be one of the sequence’s subjects.
themes.development: It surfaces as envy in 29, as professional insecurity in the rival poems, and as anger at public judgement in 111 and 121.

themes.name: Lies and self-deception
themes.summary: The poems are at their most modern when the speaker catches himself. He forgives what he has just described as a crime, praises what he has just called false, and swears to a beauty he can see is not there.
themes.development: In 35 he argues his own case against himself; in 138 both people lie and both know; in 152 he ends the sequence by declaring himself the worse perjurer of the two.

techniques.name: The English sonnet
techniques.definition: Fourteen lines of iambic pentameter in three quatrains and a closing couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg.
techniques.inThisBook: The shape is an argument machine: three chances to state a case and two lines to settle it. Shakespeare uses the quatrains as three parallel images far more often than as three steps of logic — autumn, twilight, embers in 73 — so the couplet has to do the reasoning alone.

techniques.name: The turn
techniques.definition: The point where a sonnet changes direction, traditionally at line nine in the Italian form.
techniques.inThisBook: The English shape allows the turn to move. In 29 it falls at 'Haply I think on thee' and lifts the whole poem; in 94 it is held back to the last line so that the smell of the lilies arrives with no warning; in 116 there is no turn at all, which is part of why the poem sounds like legislation.

techniques.name: The closing couplet
techniques.definition: The final rhymed pair, which sums up, reverses or undercuts the twelve lines before it.
techniques.inThisBook: It is the sequence's most variable instrument. Sometimes it seals the poem (18), sometimes it makes a joke that redistributes the property (20), sometimes it spoils the argument it is meant to finish (35), and in 126 it is missing altogether.

techniques.name: The extended conceit
techniques.definition: A single comparison pursued through a whole poem, often from an unpoetic field such as law, accounting or agriculture.
techniques.inThisBook: Sonnet 87 runs entirely on contract law — dear, estimate, charter, bonds, patent, misprision — so that the end of a love affair is conducted as the discovery of a faulty deed. The procreation poems do the same with usury and husbandry.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Setting two terms against each other inside a line or across a pair of lines.
techniques.inThisBook: Whole poems are built from it: 'comfort and despair' in 144, the before-and-after of 129, the catalogue of what love is not in 116. The balance is what makes the couplets sound like conclusions even when they are not.

techniques.name: Personification of time
techniques.definition: Treating an abstraction as a person who can act and be addressed.
techniques.inThisBook: Time gets a scythe, a hand, a pen, lion's paws to be blunted and a fickle glass to hold. Making the enemy visible is what allows the poems to declare war on it in 15 and to negotiate with it in 126.

techniques.name: Puns
techniques.definition: Using several meanings of a word together, for wit and for argument.
techniques.inThisBook: Sonnets 135 and 136 turn on Will — desire, the young man, the poet's own name and the thing a woman is said to have — until the joke becomes a demonstration of how little a name secures. Elsewhere the puns are quieter and harder: 'lie' in 138 means both deceive and sleep with.

techniques.name: Overstatement
techniques.definition: Deliberate exaggeration, used for emphasis, not to be believed.
techniques.inThisBook: Sonnet 19 gives time permission to blunt a lion and burn the phoenix; 55 expects to outlast the masonry of princes. The scale is part of the argument: only a claim this large is worth making against time at all.

quotations.text: From fairest creatures we desire increase, That thereby beauty’s rose might never die
quotations.context: The opening lines of the sequence, before any person has been addressed.
quotations.analysis: The sequence begins with a general law, not a person: we want beautiful things to continue. 'Increase' is a farming and a banking word before it is a human one, which sets the terms for the next sixteen poems — the young man is treated as capital that is not being put to work.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 1

quotations.text: When I do count the clock that tells the time
quotations.context: The opening of the first poem in the sequence to make time itself the subject.
quotations.analysis: Ten monosyllables and a ticking rhythm. Counting the clock is pointless, since the clock is already counting, and the poem’s argument grows out of that helplessness, not out of any fact about the young man.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 12

quotations.text: And all in war with Time for love of you, As he takes from you, I engraft you new.
quotations.context: The couplet that ends the last of the poems arguing for a child.
quotations.analysis: The turn the whole sequence rests on. Up to here the answer to time was a son; from here it is the poem. ‘Engraft’ keeps the gardening language of the earlier argument, so the substitution sounds like the same plan.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 15

quotations.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate
quotations.context: The opening of the best-known poem in the sequence, immediately after the procreation group ends.
quotations.analysis: The question is rhetorical and the answer is no: the poem spends its quatrains explaining why summer is the weaker term. What looks like the most conventional compliment in English is in fact a refusal of the comparison it offers.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 18

quotations.text: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
quotations.context: The couplet of sonnet 18.
quotations.analysis: 'This' is the poem, named twice and never described. The claim is a contract with the reader: the young man survives only as long as someone is doing what you are doing now, which is why the line still works.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 18

quotations.text: Devouring Time, blunt thou the lion’s paws
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that follows the immortality claim of 18.
quotations.analysis: Having promised to defeat time, the speaker spends a poem giving it permission to destroy everything else. The bargaining is comic in scale — lions, tigers, the phoenix — and the single exception at the end is the point of it.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 19

quotations.text: A woman’s face with nature’s own hand painted, Hast thou the master mistress of my passion
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that describes the young man's beauty directly.
quotations.analysis: Two categories in one phrase, and no punctuation in 1609 to separate them. The compliment works by taking the language kept for women and handing it to a man, and the poem's feminine rhymes keep the doubleness audible through all fourteen lines.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 20

quotations.text: O! learn to read what silent love hath writ:
quotations.context: The couplet of a poem comparing the speaker to an actor who forgets his part.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is to the young man and to us. A poet who cannot speak in person asks to be read instead, which makes writing a second-best — the first time the sequence admits that the page is a substitute for presence.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 23

quotations.text: When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes, I all alone beweep my outcast state
quotations.context: The opening of the sequence's clearest poem about status and envy.
quotations.analysis: Public judgement and private misery in two lines. 'All alone' is doing the work: the shame is social, the weeping is not, and the poem's recovery will also be private — a thought, not a change in circumstances.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 29

quotations.text: Haply I think on thee, and then my state, Like to the lark at break of day arising
quotations.context: The turn of sonnet 29, after eight lines of envy.
quotations.analysis: 'Haply' means by chance: the rescue is accidental, which is why it is believable. The line lifts on 'arising' and the verse follows it, the one place in the sequence where a change of mood is audible as a change of rhythm.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 29

quotations.text: When to the sessions of sweet silent thought I summon up remembrance of things past
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that follows 29, which again makes private feeling a public procedure.
quotations.analysis: A court is convened inside a head: sessions, summon, and later cancelled debts and accounts paid. Grief is conducted as legal business until the couplet dismisses the court by remembering one person.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 30

quotations.text: Full many a glorious morning have I seen Flatter the mountain tops with sovereign eye
quotations.context: The first of the three poems that respond to an injury the sequence never specifies.
quotations.analysis: The excuse is built before the accusation. By making the young man the sun, the poem forgives him for behaving like weather, and ‘flatter’ admits that the light was never sincere in the first place.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 33

quotations.text: Roses have thorns, and silver fountains mud
quotations.context: The second line of the poem in which the speaker argues the young man's case for him.
quotations.analysis: A proverb offered as comfort, and it is the beginning of a defence that goes so far the speaker calls himself an accessory to the crime. Consolation and self-disgust arrive in the same poem, which is the sequence's characteristic move.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 35

quotations.text: Not marble, nor the gilded monuments Of princes shall outlive this powerful rhyme
quotations.context: The opening of the most confident of the immortality poems.
quotations.analysis: Horace made the claim first, and every Elizabethan reader knew it. What Shakespeare adds is the demolition: statues smeared, masonry overturned, war's fire — the monument wins by being the only thing with nothing physical to destroy.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 55

quotations.text: Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore, So do our minutes hasten to their end
quotations.context: The opening of the poem placed, in the 1609 order, at the number of minutes in an hour.
quotations.analysis: The simile does two things: it gives time a sound, and it makes each minute replace the one before. ‘Pebbled’ is the detail that stops it being a figure of speech: it is a real beach, and the poem is about standing on it.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 60

quotations.text: How with this rage shall beauty hold a plea, Whose action is no stronger than a flower?
quotations.context: Early in the poem that follows the ruin of sonnet 64.
quotations.analysis: Law again: a plea, an action, a case that cannot be won. Time is taken to court here, not argued with, and beauty’s counsel has nothing to file. The answer, when it comes, is a miracle in black ink — the weakest possible defence, named as such.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 65

quotations.text: That time of year thou mayst in me behold When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang
quotations.context: The opening of the poem in which the speaker describes his own ageing.
quotations.analysis: 'Or none, or few' corrects itself mid-line, as though the speaker is looking while he writes. The second quatrain gives him a day, the third an hour of embers: each image covers less time than the last, so the poem shortens as it goes.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 73

quotations.text: Bare ruin’d choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.
quotations.context: The fourth line of the autumn poem, completing its first image.
quotations.analysis: Branches, a gutted monastery and an empty choir stall in one phrase, written within living memory of the dissolution. The birds were singers in a building that no longer sings, which makes a private poem about age carry a national ruin inside it.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 73

quotations.text: Farewell! thou art too dear for my possessing
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that ends the affair with the young man.
quotations.analysis: 'Dear' means beloved and expensive in the same breath, and the rest of the poem is conducted in contract law — estimate, charter, patent, bonds. A love affair is dissolved as though the deeds had been faulty from the start, which is dignified and also a way of not saying goodbye.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 87

quotations.text: They that have power to hurt, and will do none
quotations.context: The opening of the sequence's coldest and most argued-over poem.
quotations.analysis: Praise with no warmth in it: the admired people are stone, unmoved, slow to temptation. Whether the poem approves of them has been argued for two centuries, and the case for irony rests entirely on the last line.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 94

quotations.text: Lilies that fester smell far worse than weeds.
quotations.context: The final line of the poem praising those who do not act.
quotations.analysis: Thirteen lines of cool admiration, then a smell. The line is a proverb Shakespeare also gave to a king in Edward III, and placed here it retracts the compliment without withdrawing it: the higher the beauty, the worse the rot.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 94

quotations.text: When in the chronicle of wasted time
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that reads old poetry as prophecy.
quotations.analysis: ‘Wasted’ means used up, not squandered. The poem makes literary history a compliment (every medieval praise of a beautiful face was an attempt at this one), and then admits that present beauty leaves its admirers without words to praise it.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 106

quotations.text: Let me not to the marriage of true minds Admit impediments
quotations.context: The opening of the poem most often read at weddings.
quotations.analysis: The words come from the marriage service, where the congregation is asked to declare impediments. The poem borrows the ceremony’s authority for a love that has no ceremony, and then defines that love entirely by what it will not do.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 116

quotations.text: Love’s not Time’s fool, though rosy lips and cheeks Within his bending sickle’s compass come
quotations.context: The third quatrain of the definition poem.
quotations.analysis: A fool is a servant kept for entertainment, so the denial is specific: love is not on time's payroll. The concession in the next line is equally specific — lips and cheeks are inside the blade's reach — which leaves love defended everywhere except the body.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 116

quotations.text: O thou, my lovely boy, who in thy power Dost hold Time’s fickle glass, his fickle hour
quotations.context: The opening of the twelve-line poem that closes the young man's part of the sequence.
quotations.analysis: The last address to him is the first to call him a boy. He holds time’s hourglass, and cannot escape it, and the poem’s six couplets, with no quatrains and no turn, read like an account being settled. In 1609 the missing couplet is printed as empty brackets.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 126

quotations.text: In the old age black was not counted fair
quotations.context: The first line of the group addressed to the woman.
quotations.analysis: The subject changes and so does the method: the poem argues about taste instead of praising. ‘Fair’ means pale, beautiful and just, and the sequence spends its last twenty-five poems pulling those meanings apart.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 127

quotations.text: The expense of spirit in a waste of shame Is lust in action
quotations.context: The opening of the one poem in the sequence that addresses nobody.
quotations.analysis: No 'I', no 'thou', until the couplet says 'none knows well'. Lust is described in its three tenses, sought, had, hated, and the absence of a speaker is the point: this is a trap the poem says everybody is in.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 129

quotations.text: My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun
quotations.context: The opening of the anti-blazon.
quotations.analysis: Every comparison the sonnet tradition had worn out is named and refused — sun, coral, snow, roses, perfume, music — and the couplet then claims that the refusal is the compliment. It works because the poem never actually describes her, only what she is not.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 130

quotations.text: Whoever hath her wish, thou hast thy ‘Will,’
quotations.context: The opening of the first of the two poems that pun on the speaker’s own name.
quotations.analysis: Will is desire, a man called William, and a sexual pun, and the poem uses all three about a dozen times. The joke is not only bawdy: a name that means 'wanting' cannot secure anything, and the poem's speaker is asking to be one of many.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 135

quotations.text: When my love swears that she is made of truth, I do believe her though I know she lies
quotations.context: The opening of a poem printed in an earlier version in The Passionate Pilgrim in 1599.
quotations.analysis: Both people are lying, both know, and the arrangement holds. 'Lies' arrives at the end of the second line carrying its other meaning, and the couplet's flattery is mutual — which makes this the sequence's most companionable poem and its least romantic.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 138

quotations.text: Two loves I have of comfort and despair, Which like two spirits do suggest me still
quotations.context: The poem that states the triangle directly; also printed in 1599.
quotations.analysis: The morality play is borrowed whole — a good angel and a bad one arguing over a soul — and then spoiled, because the speaker cannot tell which has won and does not expect to. The couplet's 'fire out' is the crudest line in the sequence and the most honest about what he is waiting to learn.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 144

quotations.text: My love is as a fever longing still For that which longer nurseth the disease
quotations.context: Late in the group, after the poems of disgust.
quotations.analysis: Desire as an illness that feeds on its own cure. The medical language lets the speaker describe himself as a patient who has sacked his doctor — reason — and the last couplet turns the diagnosis on her, swearing she is fair while calling her black as hell.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 147

quotations.text: For I have sworn thee fair; more perjured I, To swear against the truth so foul a lie.
quotations.context: The last couplet of the last poem addressed to the woman.
quotations.analysis: He has spent the group accusing her of breaking oaths and ends by declaring himself the worse perjurer. It is the closing position of the whole sequence: neither forgiveness nor blame, but an admission that the praise itself was the lie.
quotations.source: Gutenberg text of the 1609 order, sonnet 152

timeline.label: Sidney's Astrophil and Stella printed
timeline.detail: The sonnet sequence becomes the fashionable English form almost overnight; Daniel, Drayton, Spenser and others follow within five years.

timeline.label: Venus and Adonis published
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's first printed book, dedicated to the Earl of Southampton — the period when the earliest sonnets were probably written.

timeline.label: The Rape of Lucrece published
timeline.detail: A second dedication to Southampton, warmer than the first, and the last time Shakespeare put his name to a dedication.

timeline.label: Francis Meres names the sonnets
timeline.detail: Palladis Tamia refers to sugared sonnets circulating among Shakespeare's private friends, so a substantial group existed in manuscript.

timeline.label: Sonnets 138 and 144 printed in The Passionate Pilgrim
timeline.detail: The Passionate Pilgrim prints early versions of sonnets 138 and 144 under Shakespeare's name.

timeline.label: Thomas Thorpe publishes the quarto
timeline.detail: SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS is entered in the Stationers' Register on 20 May and published with the dedication to Mr. W.H. It was not reprinted for thirty-one years.

timeline.label: Benson's edition rearranges the poems
timeline.detail: John Benson reorders the sequence, runs poems together under invented titles and changes some pronouns from male to female.

timeline.label: Malone restores the 1609 text
timeline.detail: Edmond Malone prints the sonnets in their quarto order with numbers and notes, the basis of every later edition.

timeline.label: Steevens refuses to reprint them
timeline.detail: George Steevens leaves the sonnets out of his edition of Shakespeare, saying no act of parliament could make readers face them — the clearest record of eighteenth-century embarrassment.

timeline.label: Wilde's The Portrait of Mr. W. H.
timeline.detail: A story about the search for the young man that is also a defence of reading the poems as love poems between men.

timeline.label: The Variorum edition
timeline.detail: Hyder Rollins collects three centuries of commentary in two volumes and shows how little the biographical questions have been settled.

timeline.label: Duncan-Jones's Arden edition
timeline.detail: Katherine Duncan-Jones argues that the 1609 quarto was authorised by Shakespeare, reopening a question that had been treated as closed.

places.name: Wilton House, Wiltshire

places.name: Stratford-upon-Avon
places.note: Where Shakespeare's family remained through the years the sequence was written.

criticalViews.summary: Read in the 1609 order the poems describe a plot: infatuation with a young man, a rival poet, a betrayal involving a woman, and a bitter end. Editions and teaching have followed that plot for two centuries.
criticalViews.counter: The order may be Thomas Thorpe's rather than Shakespeare's, some poems sit oddly where they stand, and a narrative reading has to ignore how many of the poems are exercises on set themes.

criticalViews.position: The poems are autobiography, and the people can be identified
criticalViews.summary: The dedication to 'Mr. W.H.', the Southampton and Pembroke candidacies and the hunt for the woman treat the sequence as evidence about Shakespeare's life.
criticalViews.counter: Every identification rests on initials, dedications and dates that fit several people. The sonnet vogue of the 1590s produced hundreds of first-person poems whose speakers nobody mistakes for their authors.

criticalViews.position: The immortality claims are conventional boasting
criticalViews.summary: Horace and Ovid had made the same promise; Elizabethan poets repeated it as a formula, and Shakespeare uses it at least a dozen times.
criticalViews.counter: The claim is conventional and has also turned out to be true, which the poems half anticipate: 17 imagines future readers calling the verse a liar, and 55 names the monuments it expects to outlast.

essayQuestions.question: How far do the sonnets present poetry as a defence against time?
essayQuestions.focus: Time, writing and the limits of the boast
plan: Start with the substitution in sonnet 15, where the child of the first seventeen poems is replaced by the verse itself.
Take 55 as the confident version: marble and gilded monuments named so that the rhyme can outlast them.
Set 60 against it, where the waves keep coming and the verse stands only in hope.
Use 126, which ends the young man's sequence by handing him to Time's audit and stopping two lines short.
Close on 17's worry that readers will believe the poem to be a liar, and on the fact that we are reading it.

essayQuestions.question: What does sonnet 20 do to the praise that follows it?
essayQuestions.focus: Gender, desire and the vocabulary of compliment
plan: Establish what the poem does: a woman's face, a man's heart, nature changing her mind, and a couplet that divides love from use.
Show how the surrounding poems use the language reserved for female beauty — rose, summer, fair — for a man.
Bring in the 1640 edition's changed pronouns as evidence of later discomfort.
Compare the dark lady poems, where the same vocabulary is thrown out, not transferred (130).
Conclude on whether the sequence unsettles the categories or simply borrows across them.

essayQuestions.question: Are the dark lady poems a change of subject or a change of honesty?
essayQuestions.focus: Desire, shame and the sequence's two halves
plan: Note what actually changes at 127: the addressee, the tone, and the amount of physical detail.
Read 129 as the sequence's one poem with no addressee at all, and account for its plainness.
Use 138's mutual lying to compare with the forgiveness of 33-35: the same self-knowledge, differently handled.
Take 144 as the point where the two halves meet, and consider how much the triangle explains.
Decide whether the shame in the last group is new, or has been audible since 29 and 111.

essayQuestions.question: How does the shape of the English sonnet control what these poems can argue?
plan: Set out the shape and its two resources: three parallel quatrains and a two-line settlement.
Use 73 for quatrains that work as images, each shorter in span than the last.
Use 29 for a turn that rescues a poem, and 94 for one withheld until the final line.
Take 35 as a case where the couplet spoils the argument, and ask whether that is failure or honesty.
Close with 126's missing couplet, and what an unfinished form says at the end of a sequence about endings.

discussionQuestions: The young man never speaks. Does his silence make him a character or a surface?
Which is the more convincing love poem, 116 or 138, and what does your answer say about what you want from love poetry?
Sonnet 130 will not use the usual comparisons. Is it a compliment?
If the 1609 order is a printer's rather than a poet's, does reading the poems as a story become a mistake?
Sonnet 94 praises people who feel nothing and then mentions the smell of rotting lilies. What has happened between line twelve and line thirteen?
The speaker calls his own profession a stain on his name. How much of the sequence is about work?

related.why: The narrative poem Shakespeare published first, in 1593, with the same vocabulary of beauty, refusal and pursuit.
Its companion of 1594, and the other place where Shakespeare writes at length in stanzas.
A play that builds a shared sonnet into the lovers' first meeting, written while the sequence was in progress.
Desire that crosses the categories sonnet 20 plays with, worked out as a plot.
Bad love poetry pinned to trees, and a heroine who takes it apart — Shakespeare's comedy about the sonnet habit.
